Chapter 8: Addressing Common Questions and Misconceptions
Let’s be honest—whenever you step into a new spiritual practice, it’s only natural to have questions or even a few doubts.
Maybe you’re wondering if praying the Bible is really “okay.” Or you worry it could start feeling mechanical, even a little impersonal. You might run into verses that leave you scratching your head, or feel like you’re just not qualified to use Scripture in your prayers.
Here’s something to remember: the heart of this practice isn’t about getting it perfect or ticking off boxes. It’s about relationship, not performance. The goal isn’t to master some technique—it’s to connect with God in a way that’s honest and personal.
There’s no one-size-fits-all approach to praying the Bible. This is meant to be flexible, something you can adapt to your own rhythm and needs.
Let’s walk through a few of the most common questions people have:
First up— is it okay to paraphrase or personalize the words of Scripture in prayer? Absolutely. In fact, that’s the point. You don’t have to recite every verse word-for-word. Let the words inspire you, shape your own thoughts and feelings. Make them your own—adapt them so they fit your life and your situation right now.
What if you come across a passage you just don’t understand? That happens to everyone. If a verse feels confusing or unfamiliar, it’s totally fine to move on to another part of the text. Or maybe just pause and ask God to help you understand, even if it takes time. Remember, the focus is on engaging with the text, not becoming an expert overnight.
Now, can this practice ever become routine or rote? Sure, like any habit, sometimes it can start to feel a little stale. If that happens, try mixing things up—read from a different book of the Bible, use a new translation, or find a fresh setting. The key is to bring a sense of openness and curiosity each time. Let the text surprise you, challenge you, even shake things up a bit.
And what about those difficult or troubling passages? Not every verse is easy to pray. When you hit something challenging, bring your questions and emotions honestly to God. It’s okay to wrestle, to lament, or to feel confused. The Bible itself is full of prayers just like that—ones that question, struggle, and seek understanding.
By taking these concerns seriously and responding with gentleness and honesty, this practice becomes a lot more accessible—and a lot more real.
It’s all about relationship, growth, and discovery, not about achieving some perfect outcome. And that’s what makes praying the Bible such a powerful way to grow in your faith.
